claims.evidence: MedlinePlus: used to prevent nausea and vomiting from cancer chemotherapy, radiation therapy and surgery; UK leaflets list chemo/radiotherapy and post-operative uses (emc leaflet search results).
MedlinePlus: serotonin 5-HT3 receptor antagonist class; Notts NHS sheet: dose-related QT lengthening; MHRA DSU (Jan 2020): small increased cleft risk after first-trimester use.
emc SmPC snippets: chemotherapy use in children from 6 months; radiotherapy leaflet use limited to adults, so age limits differ.
emc leaflets and MedlinePlus list prevention of post-operative nausea and vomiting.
Gut and central nervous system wording only seen in patent texts, not in the NHS sheet text retrieved. MedlinePlus says it interferes with serotonin.
claims.newSentence: Ondansetron belongs to a group called serotonin 5-HT3 receptor antagonists, which interfere with serotonin, a natural substance that can cause nausea and vomiting.

claims.evidence: MedlinePlus (via search summary): interferes with serotonin, a naturally occurring chemical that can provoke nausea and vomiting. 'Blocking' softened to 'interfering'.
emc 4 mg tablet leaflet: headache very common (more than 1 in 10).
emc leaflet: flushing and constipation common; GOSH lists warm flushes, headaches, constipation.
Leaflet/SmPC: hiccups and low blood pressure uncommon. Irregular heartbeat as an uncommon effect not seen in retrieved text.
claims.newSentence: Hiccups and low blood pressure are listed as uncommon effects.

claims.evidence: Leaflet: allergic reactions and sudden chest pain or chest tightness seen; 'heart rhythm disturbances' only in blended summary, not clearly in leaflet.
claims.newSentence: Allergic reactions and sudden chest pain or chest tightness are among the serious effects listed in a UK leaflet.

claims.evidence: Signposting rule; names 999/A&E, NHS 111, GP, pharmacist.
emc orodispersible leaflet: apomorphine (Parkinson's) listed as not to be taken with ondansetron; allergy exclusion is standard leaflet content.
emc oral solution leaflet (pil.13787): first three months of pregnancy listed as a reason not to take it.
MHRA Drug Safety Update Jan 2020: small increased risk of oral clefts after use in first 12 weeks; women to be counselled on benefits and risks if offered.
claims.newSentence: The MHRA has warned of a small increased risk of cleft lip or palate after use in the first 12 weeks of pregnancy, and says women should be counselled on the benefits and risks if it is offered.

claims.evidence: SPS: can be used with caution during breastfeeding, with monitoring (drowsiness, poor feeding, urinary retention). emc SmPC and leaflet advise mothers not to breastfeed; conflict not mentioned.
claims.newSentence: An NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service page says ondansetron can be used with caution during breastfeeding, with monitoring of the baby. UK manufacturer leaflets, by contrast, advise against breastfeeding during treatment.

claims.evidence: emc leaflets: tell doctor first about gut blockage, severe constipation, heart failure/irregular heartbeat, liver problems, potassium/sodium/magnesium problems.
NHS prescribing resource/UK labelling: QT lengthening dose-dependent; TdP reported post-marketing. 'Mainly with high IV doses' not seen in NHS text (FDA 32 mg IV statement was in a trial document).
claims.newSentence: An NHS prescribing sheet says ondansetron lengthens the QT interval (a measure of the heart's electrical cycle) in a dose-related way, and that torsade de pointes, a dangerous heart rhythm, has been reported.

claims.evidence: Notts sheet: do not prescribe in congenital QT prolongation; hypokalaemia/hypomagnesaemia corrected before use; UK labelling: caution with heart failure, bradyarrhythmias, other QT-prolonging drugs.
Notts sheet names SSRIs and SNRIs for serotonin syndrome; opioids not confirmed in the sheet text retrieved.
claims.newSentence: The sheet also warns of serotonin syndrome when ondansetron is combined with serotonergic medicines such as SSRIs and SNRIs.

claims.evidence: Notts sheet: hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia should be corrected before ondansetron.
Caution with other QT-prolonging medicines is in UK labelling and the NHS resource.
Oral solution SmPC shows POM; emc listing for 101020 specifically was not seen, though POM is standard across emc ondansetron products.
claims.newSentence: Ondansetron is a prescription-only medicine in the UK; the emc lists its oral solution as POM (prescription only medicine).

notes: Searches: 14 of 16. Leaflet URLs cited by author (pil.10159, product/101020/smpc) did not come back in my searches; equivalent emc leaflets (5216, 5222, 10160, 101020, 13787) show the same content, so URL swaps were proposed. GOSH and Notts pages only seen via search summaries, not full text. Conflict: SPS says ondansetron usable with caution in breastfeeding, whereas emc SmPC/leaflets advise mothers not to breastfeed; sentences now mention both. Pregnancy: emc SmPC/leaflet says not to use in first trimester; MHRA says counsel on risk; some formularies say avoid/prefer outside first trimester; MHRA wording is about 'first 12 weeks'. Age limits (chemo from 6 months; radiotherapy/PONV adult-only for tablets per leaflet, with inconsistent paediatric wording) should be checked by a reviewer. Opioids and 'mainly high IV doses' (FDA 16 mg single IV dose limit, 32 mg withdrawn) were not confirmed from NHS sources. Sentence 32 (999/111) is a routing rule, reworded descriptively.
